Overview — Part 1

1. General Features of Restrictive (Chronic Interstitial) Lung Disease

Restrictive lung disease is a chronic, progressive process (contrast with diffuse alveolar damage / hyaline membrane disease in ARDS, which Kemp calls an acute restrictive process). Clinically it presents with a slowly progressive, nonproductive cough and dyspnea, with dry ("Velcro") crackles on auscultation — dry because the underlying process is fibrosis/scarring, not mucus hypersecretion (there is no goblet cell hyperplasia here, unlike obstructive disease).

Pulmonary function tests: both FEV1 and FVC fall together, because scarred alveolar septa impair both the ability of the lung to fill and to empty. The FEV1/FVC ratio therefore stays roughly normal (or increases) — this is the single most important PFT distinction from obstructive disease, where the ratio decreases.

Kemp's exam hintRestrictive = decreased FEV1 and decreased FVC, normal/increased ratio. Obstructive = decreased ratio. Don't mix these up on a PFT question.

Key cytokine: transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) is repeatedly emphasized as the principal driver of the fibrosis common to nearly all of these diseases.

Gross & microscopic hallmarks

  • Cobblestone pleural surface — a shared gross feature across most restrictive lung diseases.
  • Honeycomb change — large, variably sized air spaces lined by bronchiolar-type epithelium and filled with mucus. Grossly and even microscopically at low power this can look identical to emphysema.
Honeycomb change vs. emphysemaBoth show large cystic air spaces. The distinguishing move is palpation: honeycomb change is firm because the tissue between the spaces is dense scar (fibrosis); emphysematous lung is spongy because there is pure loss of parenchyma with no fibrosis.

Complications

Progressive fibrosis destroys the alveolar septal capillary bed. Less pulmonary vasculature through which the right ventricle can pump → the right heart must work harder → pulmonary hypertension → cor pulmonale (right heart failure). This same endpoint recurs at the end of nearly every disease in this lecture, however different the starting exposure.

Kemp's classification scheme

Restrictive lung disease, by mechanism
CategoryDiseases
FibrosingUIP/IPF · NSIP · Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP) · Collagen vascular disease-associated · Pneumoconiosis · Therapy-related (drug/radiation)
GranulomatousSarcoidosis · Hypersensitivity pneumonitis
EosinophilicLoeffler syndrome · Drug-allergy related · Idiopathic chronic eosinophilic pneumonia · (Acute eosinophilic pneumonia)
Smoking-relatedRespiratory bronchiolitis-ILD · Desquamative interstitial pneumonia (DIP)
Check yourself — 2 questions
Q. A 62-year-old man with progressive dyspnea over 18 months undergoes pulmonary function testing. Which pattern is most consistent with a restrictive process?
Restrictive disease impairs both filling and emptying of the fibrotic lung, so FEV1 and FVC fall proportionally and the FEV1/FVC ratio stays normal to slightly increased. A decreased ratio is the signature of obstructive disease.
Q. An autopsy specimen shows lung with large, cystic-appearing air spaces on gross section. On palpation, the tissue is notably firm rather than spongy. This finding is most consistent with which process?
Honeycomb change looks grossly similar to emphysema (large air spaces) but is firm to palpation because of the dense fibrous tissue between the spaces; true emphysema is spongy because parenchyma is simply lost, with no fibrosis.
Fibrosing ILD

2. Usual Interstitial Pneumonia (UIP / Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis)

Demographics: more common in men, typically presents after age 50, and — unlike NSIP — is associated with smoking and other environmental exposures.

Etiology: largely unknown (Kemp notes this is actually convenient for testing — "you can't ask somebody something [that isn't known]"). Associations that have been found: mutations in telomerase genes (accelerate cellular aging → earlier end-stage fibrosis) and mutations in surfactant genes (loss of surfactant's septal-stabilizing effect may promote fibrosis, analogous to hyaline membrane disease/ARDS).

Histology — the key concept is temporal heterogeneity

UIP shows both old (dense, acellular) fibrosis and new, active fibroblast foci side by side in the same biopsy — lesions of different ages coexisting. This is the single most testable histologic discriminator from NSIP (below), which shows lesions that are all the same age.

  • Fibroblast foci: patchy, hypocellular (few cells, lots of matrix), slightly bluish proliferations of myofibroblasts within the alveolar septum.
  • Classically subpleural and paraseptal in distribution.
Sampling pearl (Kemp's residency anecdote)For most lung pathology you sample tissue around the larger vessels and airways, not the pleural surface, because that's where most pathology occurs. UIP is an exception — it characteristically starts just under the pleura, so subpleural sampling matters here specifically.

Gross: cobblestone pleural surface, honeycomb change. Prognosis: progressive and generally poor.

Check yourself — 3 questions
Q. A 58-year-old male smoker presents with progressive dyspnea and dry cough over 2 years. Lung biopsy shows patchy fibrosis of varying ages, with areas of dense old scar adjacent to pale, hypocellular fibroblastic proliferations within the alveolar septa, most prominent just beneath the pleura. Which of the following best describes this histologic pattern?
This is classic usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP): temporally heterogeneous fibrosis (old scar plus fresh fibroblast foci of different ages) concentrated in a subpleural, paraseptal distribution.
Q. Which factor is most useful in distinguishing usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) from nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) on clinical grounds?
UIP is associated with smoking/environmental exposure and is more common in men; NSIP is not smoking-associated and is more common in nonsmoking women, often with an underlying autoimmune disease.
Q. A mutation in which class of genes has been associated with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, purportedly by accelerating cellular senescence?
Telomerase gene mutations shorten telomere maintenance capacity, accelerating cellular aging and contributing to earlier fibrotic end-stage change in IPF/UIP.
Fibrosing ILD

3. Nonspecific Interstitial Pneumonia (NSIP)

Demographics: often associated with autoimmune disease, especially rheumatoid arthritis; seen in nonsmoking females, generally older individuals (similar age range to UIP) but is not associated with smoking.

Histology

  • Two variants: cellular (interstitial chronic inflammation predominates) or fibrosing (fibrosis predominates).
  • All lesions are of the same age — temporal homogeneity, the direct opposite of UIP's temporal heterogeneity.

Prognosis: better than UIP.

Differential pitfall Kemp flagsDiffuse interstitial fibrosis in NSIP can superficially resemble atypical adenomatous hyperplasia (a precursor of adenocarcinoma), but NSIP is diffuse throughout the lung rather than a discrete area — and image-based exam questions will be unambiguous, not this level of subtlety.
Check yourself — 1 question
Q. A 46-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis and no smoking history presents with progressive dyspnea. Biopsy shows interstitial fibrosis that appears uniform in age throughout the sample, without areas of dense old scar juxtaposed to fresh fibroblastic foci. Which diagnosis is most likely?
Temporally homogeneous interstitial fibrosis in a nonsmoking woman with an autoimmune disease (RA) is the classic profile for NSIP, which carries a better prognosis than UIP.
Fibrosing ILD — formerly “BOOP”

4. Cryptogenic Organizing Pneumonia (COP)

The older term, bronchiolitis obliterans organizing pneumonia (BOOP), was retired because "bronchiolitis obliterans" was easily confused with chronic bronchitis and its effects — a different, obstructive process.

Concept

This is the histologic pattern seen when a resolving pneumonia organizes into fibrous plugs within the air spaces rather than resolving cleanly.

  • If the pattern is found in a patient with a known preceding pneumonia (e.g., S. aureus, S. pneumoniae), it is simply called organizing pneumonia.
  • If the identical histologic pattern is found with no identifiable preceding cause, it is cryptogenic organizing pneumonia — "cryptogenic" literally meaning of unknown origin.
Histology vs. UIPThe organizing plugs of COP (Masson bodies) sit within the air spaces, with low cellularity and a mixed, fibromyxoid appearance — distinct from UIP's fibroblast foci, which sit within the alveolar septa. Same-sounding “fibroblastic proliferation” language, different compartment — a favorite way to test this pair.
Check yourself — 2 questions
Q. A patient develops fever, cough, and dyspnea with no prior identifiable pulmonary infection. Lung biopsy reveals polypoid plugs of loose, hypocellular fibromyxoid tissue filling the alveolar air spaces and alveolar ducts. There is no history of preceding pneumonia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
This organizing-pneumonia histologic pattern (Masson bodies filling air spaces) without an identifiable preceding cause defines cryptogenic organizing pneumonia; the identical pattern with a known antecedent infection would simply be called organizing pneumonia.
Q. Masson bodies, the intraluminal fibrous plugs of organizing pneumonia, are located in which anatomic compartment, distinguishing them from the fibroblast foci of UIP?
Masson bodies fill the intra-alveolar and alveolar duct air spaces, whereas UIP's fibroblast foci occur within the alveolar septum itself.
Fibrosing ILD

5. Collagen Vascular Disease-Associated Interstitial Lung Disease

Because collagen vascular (autoimmune) diseases share overlapping immune activation against the body's own tissues, a degree of pulmonary overlap between them is expected — particularly serositis (pleuritis/pleural effusion) as a shared feature.

Pulmonary manifestations by disease
DiseasePulmonary Findings
Rheumatoid arthritisPleuritis (± effusion), pneumonitis with fibrosis, rheumatoid nodules, pulmonary hypertension. Caplan syndrome = rheumatoid nodules in the peripheral lungs of a coal miner (RA + coal dust exposure).
Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma)Pleuritis, NSIP pattern of fibrosis.
Systemic lupus erythematosusPleuritis (± effusion), pneumonitis of mild to severe degree.
Fair-question ruleKemp explicitly notes it would be unfair to test which collagen vascular disease is present without giving you the antibody profile or other supporting clues — expect the vignette to hand you the diagnosis (or serology) and ask about the pulmonary complication, not the reverse.
Check yourself — 1 question
Q. A 55-year-old coal miner with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis is found to have well-circumscribed nodules in the peripheral lung fields on chest imaging. Which term describes this specific association?
Caplan syndrome is the combination of rheumatoid arthritis with coal dust (or other pneumoconiosis-causing) exposure, producing rheumatoid nodules in the peripheral lung.
Fibrosing ILD — occupational

6. Pneumoconioses & Coal Workers' Pneumoconiosis

Pneumoconiosis = lung disease caused by inhalation of an inorganic (or organic) particle or chemical fume. The three that Robbins — and this exam — focus on are carbon, silica, and asbestos. Others exist (beryllium → non-caseating granulomas that mimic sarcoid; byssinosis from cotton dust; stannosis from tin oxide; siderosis from iron) but are lower yield.

Coal Workers' Pneumoconiosis (CWP)

Exposure: coal miners. Pigment accumulates as pulmonary anthracosis.

Simple vs. complicated CWP
Simple CWPComplicated CWP / Progressive Massive Fibrosis (PMF)
FindingsDiscrete coal macules/nodulesLarge, confluent, densely fibrotic conglomerate scars
SymptomsUsually asymptomaticSymptomatic, significant restrictive disease
High-yield contrastCWP carries no increased risk of cancer — this is the key distinction from silicosis and asbestosis, which both do increase cancer risk. CWP can still be associated with rheumatoid arthritis/Caplan syndrome.

Kemp's teaching anecdote: even a lung that is diffusely and heavily pigmented on gross exam may cause little functional impairment, since only a fraction of total lung parenchyma is required for adequate oxygenation — underscoring why "simple" CWP is so often clinically silent despite dramatic gross findings.

Check yourself — 2 questions
Q. Which of the following is the best-established distinction between coal workers' pneumoconiosis and both silicosis and asbestosis?
A key testable distinction: coal workers' pneumoconiosis does not increase cancer risk, whereas both silicosis and asbestos-related disease do.
Q. A 61-year-old former coal miner has a chest CT showing multiple small discrete pigmented nodules scattered through both lungs. He is asymptomatic with normal pulmonary function testing. Which of the following best characterizes his condition?
Discrete, asymptomatic nodules with normal PFTs in a coal miner describe simple CWP; complicated CWP/PMF produces large confluent fibrotic masses with significant symptoms.
Fibrosing ILD — occupational

7. Silicosis

Exposure: sandblasting, mining. Distribution: characteristically the upper lobes, with a subpleural pattern.

Risk associations

  • Increased risk of carcinoma (like asbestos, unlike coal).
  • Increased risk of tuberculosis — a distinctive, standalone association not shared with the other pneumoconioses covered. Practically: clinicians monitor silicosis patients more closely for TB (e.g., PPD testing) even though it doesn't otherwise change the primary disease.
Fibrogenic driverAs with the other fibrosing diseases in this lecture, TGF-β is the main cytokine driving the fibrotic response.
Check yourself — 2 questions
Q. A 50-year-old man with 20 years of sandblasting exposure presents with gradually worsening dyspnea. Chest imaging reveals reticular and nodular opacities in the upper lobes. Which cytokine is primarily responsible for the fibrosis in this condition?
TGF-beta is the principal fibrogenic cytokine driving the fibrotic response in silicosis, as in most of the restrictive fibrosing lung diseases.
Q. Which infectious complication is classically associated with silicosis but not with coal workers' pneumoconiosis or asbestosis?
Silicosis carries a distinct, well-established increased risk for tuberculosis, thought to relate to impaired macrophage function from silica particle ingestion; this is not a feature of CWP or asbestosis.
Fibrosing ILD — occupational

8. Asbestos-Related Disease

Exposure: mining, insulation work (including demolition of older insulated buildings), shipyards, railroad engine insulation removal.

Fiber types

Chrysotile vs. amphibole fibers
FiberShapeBehaviorPathogenicity
Chrysotile ("serpentine")Curved, curlyImpacts higher in the airway — more easily cleared by mucociliary actionLess pathogenic (most common fiber, but least damaging)
AmphiboleStraightPenetrates farther into the lung parenchyma/alveoli, very difficult to clear once thereMore pathogenic (main driver of disease)

Pleural plaques — a marker of exposure, not disease

Pleural plaques are flat, off-white, dense fibrotic plaques on the pleural (including diaphragmatic) surface. They do not themselves cause disease/dysfunction — they simply mark asbestos exposure. (Other exposures can rarely cause pleural plaques too, so a full exposure history still matters.)

Asbestos exposure ≠ asbestosisAsbestos exposure just means the patient has been exposed (may have pleural plaques, and carries increased cancer risk regardless). Asbestosis specifically means the patient has developed the restrictive lung disease — i.e., established pulmonary fibrosis. Don't conflate the two terms.

Asbestosis

Other features: pleural effusions and dense pleural adhesions (can be striking enough that the lung must be dissected free from the chest wall en bloc at autopsy).

Ferruginous (asbestos) bodies — the hallmark finding

Macrophages cannot degrade the fiber, so they coat it in iron and protein, producing the classic beaded/dumbbell appearance. The straight shape reflects the more pathogenic amphibole fiber.

Malignancy risk

  • Malignant mesothelioma (pleural, and rarely pericardial/peritoneal) — per Kemp: pleural mesothelioma is asbestos exposure until proven otherwise; there is essentially no other common cause.
  • Bronchogenic carcinoma (can be any histologic type, including squamous cell carcinoma).
Synergy with smoking — the single most tested number in this sectionSmoking alone carries roughly a 10× increased risk of lung cancer; asbestos exposure alone roughly 5×. Combined, the risk is roughly 50× (Kemp cites ~50–55×) — far more than simply additive (10 + 5 = 15). This is a true synergistic interaction, and it's one of the few numeric relationships Kemp explicitly flags as testable.
Check yourself — 3 questions
Q. An autopsy identifies numerous straight, golden-brown, beaded fibers coated with iron and protein within the lung parenchyma, along with dense septal fibrosis and honeycomb change. Which fiber type is most likely responsible for this pathology?
Ferruginous (asbestos) bodies form around fibers, and the straight morphology corresponds to amphibole fibers, which penetrate deeper into the alveolar parenchyma and are more pathogenic than the curly, more easily cleared chrysotile fibers.
Q. A 64-year-old former shipyard worker with a 40-year, 1-pack-per-day smoking history and documented asbestos exposure is found to have a markedly increased risk of bronchogenic carcinoma compared to the general population. Which best describes the nature of the interaction between these two risk factors?
Smoking (~10x) and asbestos (~5x) combine synergistically to produce roughly a 50-55x increased risk of bronchogenic carcinoma, far greater than the simple sum of the two individual risks.
Q. Which statement correctly distinguishes 'asbestos exposure' from 'asbestosis'?
Exposure alone (which may show pleural plaques and increased cancer risk) does not equal disease; asbestosis specifically denotes the fibrotic restrictive lung disease that can result from that exposure.
Part 2 — Restrictive Pulmonary Disorders, continued
Fibrosing ILD — iatrogenic

9. Drug- and Radiation-Induced Pulmonary Fibrosis

Amiodarone is highlighted as, in Kemp's autopsy experience, by far the most common drug cause of restrictive lung disease he has personally encountered. His summary of its reputation: "cardiologists love it, and everybody else hates it."

Certain chemotherapeutic agents can also produce pulmonary fibrosis, as can radiation therapy, through direct tissue damage and scarring.

Underlying mechanismAs with the other fibrosing entities in this lecture, the shared final pathway is fibrosis of the alveolar septa — drug- and radiation-induced disease simply represents a different upstream trigger for the same downstream process.
Check yourself — 1 question
Q. An elderly patient on long-term therapy for atrial fibrillation develops progressive dyspnea. Autopsy reveals an irregular, bumpy pleural surface and diffusely thickened, fibrotic alveolar septa. Which medication is most likely responsible?
Amiodarone is the most common drug-related cause of restrictive/fibrotic lung disease encountered at autopsy in this lecture's teaching experience, producing diffuse septal fibrosis.
Granulomatous ILD

10. Sarcoidosis

Etiology: unknown — genetically predisposed individuals with immune dysregulation. Kemp notes this actually makes it a favorable exam topic precisely because there's no single confirmed cause to interrogate. The immune response is driven by CD4+ T-helper 1 (Th1) cells (contrast with the Th2-driven response of asthma).

Granulomas

  • Non-caseating granulomas (contrast tuberculosis, which is classically caseating) — "usually, but not absolute."
  • Granulomas = collections of epithelioid histiocytes (enlarged macrophages with abundant cytoplasm and small nuclei); giant cells may or may not be present — giant cells are not required to call something a granuloma.

Associated microscopic findings (not required for diagnosis)

  • Asteroid bodies — stellate (star-shaped) eosinophilic inclusions found within giant cells.
  • Schaumann bodies — laminated, calcified concretions (basophilic/bluish on H&E), seen less often than asteroid bodies in Kemp's experience.
Not pathognomonicNeither asteroid nor Schaumann bodies are specific for sarcoidosis — they occur in other granulomatous conditions too — but they are classic associated findings worth recognizing.

Staging & pulmonary course

Disease can be staged by what's involved: hilar lymphadenopathy alone (best prognosis, parenchyma spared) up through progression to pulmonary parenchymal fibrosis, which — like the other fibrosing diseases — leads to pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale.

In advanced pulmonary sarcoidosis, the same fibrosis-→pulmonary-hypertension-→cor pulmonale sequence applies as in the other restrictive diseases.

Extrapulmonary involvement

Organ involvement in sarcoidosis
SiteFinding
SkinErythema nodosum (red, tender/hemorrhagic nodules, typically on the legs — no granulomas here) vs. subcutaneous nodules (which do contain granulomas)
EyeUveitis, iritis, choroiditis, optic nerve involvement
Eye + salivary glandsSicca syndrome (dry eyes/dry mouth)
Uveoparotid involvementHeerfordt syndrome
HeartPatchy myocardial scarring mimicking an old MI, but with minimal/no coronary artery disease to explain it
OtherSpleen, liver, bone marrow (reportedly spares the adrenal gland)

Labs

  • Hypercalcemia / hypercalciuria — granuloma macrophages activate vitamin D, which drives calcium (and phosphate) absorption for bone formation.
  • Elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) — roughly tracks with overall disease burden, so can be followed clinically alongside treatment.
Check yourself — 3 questions
Q. A 34-year-old Black woman presents with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on chest imaging, hypercalcemia, and an elevated serum ACE level. Lung biopsy shows non-caseating granulomas. Which cell type is central to the pathogenesis of this disease?
Sarcoidosis granuloma formation is driven by CD4+ Th1 cells, in contrast to the Th2-predominant response seen in asthma.
Q. A patient with known sarcoidosis develops tender, red nodules on both shins. Biopsy of a similar lesion elsewhere on a different patient with subcutaneous sarcoid nodules would be expected to show granulomas, but biopsy of erythema nodosum itself shows which finding?
Erythema nodosum, though associated with sarcoidosis, does not itself contain granulomas; it reflects a nonspecific inflammatory reaction in the subcutaneous fat, unlike true subcutaneous sarcoid nodules.
Q. Sarcoid granulomas are found to contain stellate, eosinophilic, star-shaped inclusions within giant cells on histologic exam. What is this specific finding called?
The stellate eosinophilic inclusion within a giant cell is called an asteroid body, a classic (though non-specific) associated finding in sarcoidosis; Schaumann bodies are laminated calcified concretions, a separate finding.
Granulomatous ILD

11. Hypersensitivity Pneumonitis

An immunologic hypersensitivity reaction to an inhaled organic antigen. Several named exposure-specific forms exist (memorizing every name isn't required, but recognizing the exposure pattern is):

  • Farmer's lung — thermophilic actinomycetes in moldy hay/dust.
  • Pigeon breeder's (bird fancier's) lung — avian proteins.
  • Humidifier lung — thermophilic bacteria colonizing heater/humidifier water reservoirs.
History-taking pearlKemp explicitly frames this as the reason to always ask a pulmonary patient about hobbies and occupational exposures, not just their job title.

Pathogenesis: immune-mediated, with increased CD4+ and CD8+ T cells and antibody formation; the precise mechanism is still being worked out.

Histology

  • Ill-defined, peribronchiolar (bronchiolocentric) granulomas — deliberately vaguer/less discrete than sarcoid granulomas.
  • Interstitial inflammation with granulomas in the interstitium.
  • Late-stage: interstitial fibrosis and honeycomb change (converging, at the end stage, with the other fibrosing diseases — making etiology hard to pin down once end-stage fibrosis is reached without a known prior exposure history).

Acute vs. chronic presentation

AcuteChronic
Fever, dyspnea, cough within hours of a discrete exposure; increased WBC count; restrictive pattern on PFTsProgressive dyspnea over time, cyanosis, poor oxygenation; decreased total lung compliance from the scarred, poorly distensible alveolar walls
Check yourself — 2 questions
Q. A 31-year-old man develops fever, cough, and dyspnea approximately 6 hours after his first day cleaning out central heating/air ducts. Lung biopsy would most likely reveal which histologic pattern?
Acute exposure to thermophilic bacteria in ductwork/humidifier reservoirs causing rapid-onset symptoms is classic for acute hypersensitivity pneumonitis, which shows ill-defined, bronchiolocentric (peribronchiolar) granulomas.
Q. A pigeon breeder develops chronic, progressive dyspnea and cyanosis over several years. Pulmonary function testing shows a restrictive pattern with decreased total lung compliance. Which of the following underlying histologic changes best explains the decreased compliance?
Chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis progresses to interstitial fibrosis; scarred, poorly distensible alveolar walls reduce lung compliance, producing the restrictive physiology and worsening gas exchange over time.
Eosinophilic ILD

12. Eosinophilic Lung Diseases

Eosinophils play a role across a range of pulmonary conditions:

  • Loeffler syndrome — caused by migrating helminth larvae (classically Strongyloides, also others such as Ascaris) passing through the lung, producing transient infiltrates and peripheral eosinophilia. Remember the classic triad of causes of eosinophilia: drugs, parasites, and (per this category) asthma/allergic disease.
  • Secondary eosinophilia — a prominent component of asthma (all types), drug allergy reactions, and vasculitides with a strong eosinophilic trigger (e.g., eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis).
  • Idiopathic chronic eosinophilic pneumonia — essentially a diagnosis of exclusion; not well characterized mechanistically.
  • Acute eosinophilic pneumonia — rapid onset, can be serious enough to progress to respiratory failure; chest x-ray shows infiltrates; bronchoalveolar lavage reveals abundant eosinophils; histology shows diffuse alveolar damage.
General pattern for interpreting any of these on a vignetteAcute processes present with rapid onset ± fever, since inflammation is involved; lung involvement produces dyspnea; and severe acute cases can progress quickly to respiratory failure with x-ray infiltrates.
Check yourself — 2 questions
Q. A patient recently returned from a rural area with a history of chronic soil exposure presents with transient pulmonary infiltrates and peripheral eosinophilia. Migration of which organism through the lungs is the classic cause of this presentation?
Loeffler syndrome is classically caused by migrating helminth larvae, with Strongyloides being the most frequently cited organism, producing transient infiltrates with peripheral eosinophilia.
Q. A young woman develops sudden-onset dyspnea, fever, and diffuse infiltrates on chest x-ray, rapidly progressing to respiratory failure. Bronchoalveolar lavage shows a marked eosinophilia, and lung biopsy shows diffuse alveolar damage. No parasitic, drug, or vasculitic cause is identified. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Acute eosinophilic pneumonia presents with rapid-onset severe respiratory symptoms that can progress to respiratory failure, with BAL eosinophilia and diffuse alveolar damage on histology.
Smoking-related ILD

13. Smoking-Related Interstitial Lung Disease (RB-ILD & DIP)

Pulmonary anthracosis

Normal lung should appear pink-tan. Black surface discoloration is anthracosis — most often from cigarette smoking, though heavy environmental/occupational smoke exposure can also cause it. By itself, anthracosis typically causes no underlying disease — it does not imply emphysema or fibrosis on its own.

Respiratory bronchiolitis

Pigmented macrophage accumulation centered on the bronchioles. On its own this finding alone doesn't necessarily cause disease, but when it progresses to include fibrosis, it evolves toward an interstitial lung disease — termed respiratory bronchiolitis-associated interstitial lung disease (RB-ILD).

Desquamative interstitial pneumonia (DIP)

A major, diffuse accumulation of alveolar macrophages filling essentially every air space (not just peribronchiolar, unlike RB-ILD). Per Kemp's teaching, this is seen almost exclusively in cigarette smokers — a very characteristic exposure link.

Check yourself — 2 questions
Q. At autopsy, a heavy smoker's lung shows diffuse black discoloration of the pleural surface, but no fibrosis, no nodules, and normal underlying architecture. What is the clinical significance of this finding by itself?
Pulmonary anthracosis (pigment deposition from smoking or heavy smoke exposure) by itself is usually an incidental finding without associated functional impairment, distinct from fibrosing pneumoconioses.
Q. A 55-year-old current smoker undergoes lung biopsy for a nonspecific interstitial abnormality. The biopsy shows nearly every alveolar air space diffusely filled with pigmented macrophages. Which diagnosis is most consistent with this pattern and its characteristic exposure history?
DIP shows massive, diffuse filling of alveolar spaces by pigmented macrophages and is seen almost exclusively in cigarette smokers, distinguishing it from the more localized, peribronchiolar pattern of isolated respiratory bronchiolitis.
Extrinsic restriction

14. Musculoskeletal Causes of Restrictive Lung Disease

Restrictive physiology does not always originate from the lung parenchyma itself. Scoliosis (lateral curvature of the vertebral column) and kyphosis (forward curvature) can mechanically restrict chest wall and lung expansion even when the underlying lung tissue is otherwise entirely normal.

Clinical vignette from KempHe describes a medical-school patient on a ventilator solely because of severe kyphoscoliosis — the vertebral column deformity was severe enough to prevent effective breathing despite intrinsically normal lung parenchyma. This illustrates that a 'restrictive' picture on PFTs does not always mean intrinsic lung disease.
Check yourself — 1 question
Q. A patient with severe kyphoscoliosis is found to have a restrictive pattern on pulmonary function testing, but chest CT shows entirely normal lung parenchyma with no fibrosis, nodules, or honeycombing. What is the most likely explanation for the restrictive physiology?
Severe scoliosis/kyphosis can produce a restrictive pattern purely from mechanical limitation of chest wall and lung expansion, without any intrinsic parenchymal lung disease.
Rare restrictive disease

15. Pulmonary Alveolar Proteinosis (PAP)

A rare condition with a relatively well-defined pathogenesis (unlike many others in this lecture): a defect in macrophage/granulocyte clearance of surfactant, related to GM-CSF (granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor) signaling.

Forms

  • Autoimmune (most common) — antibodies directed against GM-CSF.
  • Secondary — to a variety of conditions, notably including silicosis (silica exposure is called out specifically as a secondary cause).
  • Congenital — an inherited deficiency.

Histology

Alveolar air spaces fill with granular, PAS-positive proteinaceous material derived from surfactant. The key distinguishing point from pulmonary edema on histology: PAP material has a textured/granular quality, whereas edema fluid is smooth and homogeneous.

Clinical presentation

Cough with gelatinous sputum (patients can literally cough up some of the accumulated material); recurrent respiratory infections (the accumulated proteinaceous material is an excellent culture medium for bacteria); progressive dyspnea and cyanosis. Because it is rare, diagnosis is often delayed, sometimes after several prior episodes of pneumonia.

No fibrosis (at least initially)Unlike most of this lecture's other restrictive diseases, PAP is a restrictive process from alveolar filling, not from fibrosis — though fibrosis can develop over time in some cases.
Check yourself — 2 questions
Q. A 34-year-old with a history of silicosis presents with progressive dyspnea, a chronic cough productive of gelatinous sputum, and recurrent bacterial pneumonias. Lung biopsy shows alveolar spaces filled with granular, PAS-positive material. Which of the following pathways is most directly implicated in the underlying defect?
Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis results from defective macrophage/granulocyte-mediated clearance of surfactant, most commonly via autoimmune antibodies against GM-CSF; silicosis is a recognized secondary cause.
Q. On histologic comparison, how does the intra-alveolar material of pulmonary alveolar proteinosis typically differ in appearance from pulmonary edema fluid?
PAP produces a slightly textured, granular intra-alveolar material derived from accumulated surfactant, in contrast to the smooth, homogeneous appearance of simple pulmonary edema fluid.
Parts 1 & 2 combined
